title: I'm a UX designer, not a game dev. With an AI coding assistant I shipped a 3D off-road game to iOS, Android, Mac and web in four weeks
author: flayzeraynx
selftext:
I've designed products for twenty years and had never made a game. Four weeks ago I started Hush Trail, a quiet off-road driving game, and it's now live on four platforms. Here's how the work actually split, because I think the split is the interesting part.



I did the game design, the feel, the art direction, every UI decision and all the testing on the phone, which mostly meant saying "no, that feels wrong" a lot. Claude wrote almost all of the code: roughly 43k lines of GDScript in Godot 4, covering vehicle physics, streaming terrain, shaders, menus, a multiplayer convoy and the build scripts. There is no generative AI in the assets. The models are built by Blender scripts, the plants start from a CC0 nature kit, the ambience is CC0 field recordings and the radio music is synthesized by our own scripts.



Three habits made this work. First, the whole project is text (Godot scenes and scripts), so the assistant can read and change everything. Second, the game has headless test hooks: spawn here, run this driving test, render this frame. Every change gets checked on real frames instead of on hope. Third, there's a running log file in the repo, so each new session knows what was decided and why.



Some things went further than I expected. The art for 2.0 used no image models: the assistant wrote Blender scripts that build every truck, tree, rock, cabin and cloud, plus Python that paints the textures, and I steered by looking at renders and saying what was off. The trailer is made the same way: each shot is rendered by the game from a shot list, a script checks every clip for repeated frames, and ffmpeg cuts it to the music. When a Reddit comment asked for motorcycles, three bikes (with lean, a steered fork and a rider bent onto the pegs) were in the browser build that evening.



The one I still find strange is Android. Neither of us owns an Android phone. The assistant ran the game on real phones in a cloud device lab, switched features off one at a time to find what cost the most, then wrote cheaper shader variants and dynamic resolution. Mid-range phones went from 3-12 fps to 24-35 in the lab. It also pulls the analytics and store reports itself, and last week it told me my pricing idea was aimed at the wrong problem: players were leaving in the first minute, long before they saw a price.



What didn't work: physics feel can't be judged from logs, so I had to drive it on the phone myself. Big UI changes needed several rounds of screenshots and blunt feedback. And lab numbers flattered us: real Android players still average about 20 fps.



Free to try in the browser: [https://hushtrail.app/play](https://hushtrail.app/play)

iPhone, iPad and Mac: [https://apps.apple.com/app/id6828103738](https://apps.apple.com/app/id6828103738)

Android: [https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.ozankilic.hushtrail](https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.ozankilic.hushtrail)



Happy to answer process questions.
